complete_triples.relationship: historical setting of Jehoiakim's reign
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah dates this oracle to the beginning of Jehoiakim son of Josiah's reign. Kings describes Pharaoh installing Josiah's son Eliakim, renaming him Joakim, and gives his reign's length. The father and accession setting connect the accounts while their name forms remain unchanged.

target_units.display_text: Pharaoh Nechao made Eliakim, son of Josiah king of Judah, king over them in place of his father Josiah and changed his name to Joakim. He took Joachas and brought him into Egypt, and he died there.

complete_triples.relationship: preserving the commanded word
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah must deliver every commanded word without taking one away. Deuteronomy likewise forbids taking anything from the commanded word. The shared restriction concerns faithful transmission and observance of divine instruction, with Jeremiah applying it to his public oracle.

source_unit.text: Thus said the Lord: Stand in the courtyard of the Lord’s house and deliver an oracle to all the Judeans and all who come to bow down in the Lord’s house—all the words I commanded you to deliver to them. Do not take away a word.
source_unit.display_text: Thus said the Lord: Stand in the courtyard of the Lord’s house and deliver an oracle to all the Judeans and all who come to bow down in the Lord’s house—all the words I commanded you to deliver to them. Do not take away a word.

target_units.text: You shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it; you shall keep the commandments of the Lord your God, which I command you this day.

complete_triples.relationship: repentance and the withdrawal of threatened calamity
complete_triples.rationale: The possibility that listeners turn from evil explains why the threatened calamity might cease. Jeremiah 18 states the same conditional pattern for a nation that turns from its evils: the Lord changes His announced intention to harm it.

source_unit.text: Perhaps they will hear and turn, each from his evil way, and I will cease from the evils I plan to do to them because of their evil practices.
source_unit.display_text: Perhaps they will hear and turn, each from his evil way, and I will cease from the evils I plan to do to them because of their evil practices.

target_units.display_text: and if that nation turns from all their evils, I will change My mind concerning the evils I planned to do to them.

complete_triples.relationship: hearing God and walking in His commands
complete_triples.rationale: The temple warning makes hearing the Lord and walking in His ordinances decisive. Jeremiah 7 similarly joins hearing His voice with walking in all His commanded ways. Both measure the people's response by obedience rather than their presence at the temple.

source_unit.text: And say: Thus said the Lord: If you do not hear Me, walking in My ordinances that I set before your face,
source_unit.display_text: And say: Thus said the Lord: If you do not hear Me, walking in My ordinances that I set before your face,

target_units.text: But this utterance I commanded them, saying: Hear My voice, and I will be your God and you will be My people; and walk in all My ways that I command you, so that it may be well with you.
target_units.display_text: But this utterance I commanded them, saying: Hear My voice, and I will be your God and you will be My people; and walk in all My ways that I command you, so that it may be well with you.

complete_triples.relationship: rejected prophets sent persistently
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah recalls the Lord sending His servants the prophets from early morning without being heard. Jeremiah 7 likewise describes prophets sent by day and at dawn, followed by the people's refusal to hear. The repeated sending and refusal closely correspond.

source_unit.text: listening to the words of My servants the prophets whom I send to you from early morning, and have sent—though you did not listen to Me—

target_units.display_text: From the day their fathers left Egypt’s land until this day, I sent out to you all My servants the prophets by day and at dawn, and I sent them.

target_units.text: And they did not hear Me, and their ear did not attend, and they hardened their neck beyond their fathers.
target_units.display_text: And they did not hear Me, and their ear did not attend, and they hardened their neck beyond their fathers.

complete_triples.relationship: Shiloh as a precedent for temple judgment
complete_triples.rationale: The threatened fate of the house is explicitly compared with Shiloh. Jeremiah 7 explains that precedent by directing hearers to what happened at Shiloh and announcing the same treatment for the house bearing the Lord's name.

complete_triples.relationship: narrative parallel of seizure amid temple accusations
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah is seized after delivering the temple oracle and threatened with death. Stephen is also seized, with witnesses accusing him of speaking against the holy place and its destruction. The accounts share seizure amid temple controversy; Acts explicitly calls Stephen's witnesses false.

source_unit.display_text: And when Jeremiah stopped speaking everything the Lord commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests, false prophets, and all the people seized him, saying: You must die!

complete_triples.relationship: the disputed Shiloh warning repeated
complete_triples.rationale: The accusation against Jeremiah repeats his warning that the house will become like Shiloh. Jeremiah 7 contains the corresponding warning and its stated reason in the people's deeds and refusal to hear. It supplies the content contested by Jeremiah's opponents.

complete_triples.relationship: judicial parallel of a religious death demand
complete_triples.rationale: The priests and false prophets demand a death sentence because of Jeremiah's prophecy against the city. Matthew records a high priest's charge of blasphemy and the answer that Jesus is liable to death. The parallel concerns religious accusation and a death demand, with different charges.

source_unit.text: And the priests and false prophets said to the rulers and all the people: A sentence of death for this man, because he prophesied against this city, as you heard with your own ears!
source_unit.display_text: And the priests and false prophets said to the rulers and all the people: A sentence of death for this man, because he prophesied against this city, as you heard with your own ears!

target_units.display_text: What do you think?” They answered, “He is liable to death.”

complete_triples.relationship: prophetic commission invoked in defense
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah answers the accusation by saying the Lord sent him to speak these words. His commissioning account likewise joins being sent with speaking everything commanded and receiving the Lord's words in his mouth. His defense appeals to that assigned responsibility.

source_unit.text: And Jeremiah said to the rulers and all the people: The Lord sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all these words you heard.
source_unit.display_text: And Jeremiah said to the rulers and all the people: The Lord sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all these words you heard.

target_units.text: Do not fear them, because I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord.
target_units.display_text: Do not fear them, because I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord.

target_units.display_text: The Lord stretched out His hand toward me and touched my mouth. The Lord said to me, Behold, I have put My words into your mouth.

complete_triples.relationship: reform of ways and practices
complete_triples.rationale: The appeal to improve ways and works repeats the instruction to Judah in Jeremiah 18 to turn from evil and improve practices. Both place a concrete call to reform within a warning of calamity, rather than treating the warning as unrelated to the people's response.

source_unit.text: And now make your ways and works better and hear the Lord’s voice, and the Lord will cease from the evils He spoke against you.
source_unit.display_text: And now make your ways and works better and hear the Lord’s voice, and the Lord will cease from the evils He spoke against you.

target_units.text: And now say to Judah’s men and those dwelling in Jerusalem: Behold, I am shaping evils against you and devising a design against you. Let each turn from his evil way now, and make your practices better.
target_units.display_text: And now say to Judah’s men and those dwelling in Jerusalem: Behold, I am shaping evils against you and devising a design against you. Let each turn from his evil way now, and make your practices better.

complete_triples.relationship: Jeremiah placed in others' power
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah declares that he is in his hearers' hands and leaves his treatment to them. In Jeremiah 45 the king declares him in the officials' hands because he cannot oppose them. The shared expression marks the prophet's vulnerability, although the speakers and occasions differ.

source_unit.text: And behold, I am in your hands. Do to me what is advantageous and better for you.
source_unit.display_text: And behold, I am in your hands. Do to me what is advantageous and better for you.

target_units.text: The king said, He is in your hands—for the king was unable to oppose them.
target_units.display_text: The king said, He is in your hands—for the king was unable to oppose them.

complete_triples.relationship: responsibility for a condemned man's blood
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah warns that killing him would place innocent blood on his hearers and the city. Matthew's trial scene also explicitly contests responsibility for blood: Pilate disclaims it and the crowd accepts it. The comparison concerns the narrated responsibility, not any extension of guilt beyond those scenes.

source_unit.text: But know for certain that if you kill me, you place innocent blood upon yourselves, this city, and its inhabitants, because the Lord truly sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears.
source_unit.display_text: But know for certain that if you kill me, you place innocent blood upon yourselves, this city, and its inhabitants, because the Lord truly sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears.

target_units.display_text: When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but rather an uproar was arising, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, “I am innocent of this blood. See to it yourselves.”

target_units.display_text: All the people answered, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

complete_triples.relationship: finding no charge deserving death
complete_triples.rationale: The rulers and people reject a death sentence for Jeremiah because he spoke in God's name. The official report concerning Paul likewise finds no charge deserving death or imprisonment. Both counter a lethal accusation with a stated finding, while giving different reasons.

source_unit.text: And the rulers and all the people said to the priests and false prophets: There is no sentence of death for this man, because he spoke to us in the name of the Lord our God.
source_unit.display_text: And the rulers and all the people said to the priests and false prophets: There is no sentence of death for this man, because he spoke to us in the name of the Lord our God.

complete_triples.relationship: explicit quotation of Micah's judgment oracle
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah's elders name Micah and repeat the judgment of Zion plowed as a field and the temple mountain becoming woodland. Micah contains that oracle. The supplied Jerusalem descriptions differ: Jeremiah says an untrodden place, while Micah says a fruit watcher's hut.

source_unit.text: Micah the Morathite lived in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah and said to all Judah’s people: Thus said the Lord: Zion will be plowed as a field, Jerusalem will become an untrodden place, and the house’s mountain a grove of woodland.
source_unit.display_text: Micah the Morathite lived in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah and said to all Judah’s people: Thus said the Lord: Zion will be plowed as a field, Jerusalem will become an untrodden place, and the house’s mountain a grove of woodland.

target_units.display_text: Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will be like a fruit watcher’s hut, and the mountain of the house like a forest grove.

complete_triples.relationship: judgment relented after a changed response
complete_triples.rationale: The elders recall fearing and entreating the Lord, followed by His ceasing from threatened evils in Hezekiah's time. Jonah narrates God seeing Nineveh turn from evil and withholding the announced calamity. These are distinct events sharing a responsive change in the announced judgment.

source_unit.text: Did Hezekiah and all Judah kill him? Was it not that they feared the Lord and entreated the Lord’s face, and the Lord ceased from the evils He spoke against them? And we have done great evils against our own lives!
source_unit.display_text: Did Hezekiah and all Judah kill him? Was it not that they feared the Lord and entreated the Lord’s face, and the Lord ceased from the evils He spoke against them? And we have done great evils against our own lives!

complete_triples.relationship: prophet fleeing a royal death threat
complete_triples.rationale: Uriah hears that the king and rulers seek his death and enters Egypt. Elijah also leaves to preserve his life after a royal death threat, reaching Beer-sheba. Both narratives connect a prophet's flight with royal hostility, without identifying the destinations or outcomes.

complete_triples.rationale: Jehoiakim has Uriah brought back and kills him with the sword. Chronicles describes Azarias son of Jehoiada speaking by God's Spirit and being stoned at King Joash's command. Both depict royal responsibility for killing a prophetic critic; the names and methods differ.

complete_triples.relationship: Ahikam's earlier role among royal envoys
complete_triples.rationale: Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah. Kings names Achikam son of Sapphan among the men commissioned to inquire of the Lord and sent to the prophetess Olda. complete_triples.rationale: The Lord commands Jeremiah to put bonds and collars around his neck. complete_triples.rationale: The collar message is sent to the rulers of Idumea, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon. These same peoples and rulers appear among those made to drink the judgment cup. The common recipients connect two prophetic signs without making their messages or symbols identical.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah grounds the Lord's assignment of the earth in His creative power and will. complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah says the earth and its beasts were given to Nebuchadnezzar for service. Daniel tells the Babylonian king that heaven gave him rule and handed humans and beasts into his hands. The distinctive combination of royal dominion and animals closely corresponds.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah warns nations refusing Babylon's yoke of sword, famine and destruction. Deuteronomy describes serving an enemy in deprivation with an iron collar until destruction. The shared image is imposed foreign rule; the immediate command being resisted differs between the passages.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah warns against diviners, omens and enchantments supporting the prediction that Babylon need not be served. Deuteronomy prohibits these practices and contrasts the nations' reliance on them with Israel's instruction. The overlap concerns named practices, not a claim that every dream is condemned.

target_units.display_text: The Lord showed me two baskets of figs lying before the Lord’s sanctuary, after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, the rulers, craftsmen, prisoners, and rich people from Jerusalem and brought them to Babylon.

complete_triples.relationship: the deportees addressed as people sent by the Lord
complete_triples.rationale: The letter addresses those the Lord says He deported from Jerusalem. The good-fig interpretation similarly identifies Judah's deportees as those He sent to the Chaldeans' land for good. Both frame the displaced community as the recipient of His continuing address and intention.

source_unit.text: Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God, concerning the deportees whom I deported from Jerusalem:
source_unit.display_text: Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God, concerning the deportees whom I deported from Jerusalem:

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Like these good figs, so I will acknowledge Judah’s deportees, whom I have sent from this place to the Chaldeans’ land, for good things.
target_units.display_text: Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Like these good figs, so I will acknowledge Judah’s deportees, whom I have sent from this place to the Chaldeans’ land, for good things.

complete_triples.relationship: houses inhabited and planted produce enjoyed
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah instructs deportees to build houses, dwell in them and eat what they plant. Isaiah promises people will inhabit their houses and eat their own planted produce. The activities closely correspond, although Jeremiah commands settled life in exile and Isaiah describes a promised condition.

source_unit.text: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruits,
source_unit.display_text: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruits,

target_units.text: They will build houses and inhabit them themselves; they will plant vineyards and eat their own produce.
target_units.display_text: They will build houses and inhabit them themselves; they will plant vineyards and eat their own produce.

target_units.text: They will not build for others to inhabit or plant for others to eat. For My people’s days will be like those of the tree of life; they will wear out the works of their labor.
target_units.display_text: They will not build for others to inhabit or plant for others to eat. For My people’s days will be like those of the tree of life; they will wear out the works of their labor.

target_units.text: My chosen ones will not labor in vain or bear children for a curse, because they are offspring blessed by God, and their descendants will be with them.
target_units.display_text: My chosen ones will not labor in vain or bear children for a curse, because they are offspring blessed by God, and their descendants will be with them.

complete_triples.relationship: Israel increasing while living outside its homeland
complete_triples.rationale: The deportees are told to form families, multiply and not become fewer. Exodus narrates Israel's sons multiplying and becoming numerous in Egypt. Both associate Israel's life in a foreign land with numerical increase; one is counsel and the other a narrative report.

source_unit.text: and take wives and beget sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters to husbands. Multiply and do not become fewer,
source_unit.display_text: and take wives and beget sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters to husbands. Multiply and do not become fewer,

target_units.text: And the sons of Israel increased and multiplied, and became numerous and exceedingly, exceedingly strong; and the land multiplied them.

complete_triples.relationship: prayer for society's peace and the worshippers' welfare
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah joins prayer for the receiving land with the deportees' own peace within it. First Timothy urges prayers for rulers and all people so that believers may live quietly. Both connect intercession for the wider society with the community's peaceful life.

source_unit.text: and seek the peace of the land where I deported you, and pray to the Lord for them, because in its peace you will have peace.
source_unit.display_text: and seek the peace of the land where I deported you, and pray to the Lord for them, because in its peace you will have peace.

target_units.text: Therefore I urge first of all that petitions, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made for all people,
target_units.display_text: Therefore I urge first of all that petitions, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made for all people,

target_units.text: for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and dignity.
target_units.display_text: for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and dignity.

complete_triples.relationship: refusing deceptive prophetic and divinatory assurances
complete_triples.rationale: The letter warns deportees against false prophets, diviners and dreams. Jeremiah 34 warns against the same kinds of speakers and practices when they promise freedom from Babylonian service. The repeated warning addresses deceptive guidance about the exile's course.

source_unit.text: Because thus said the Lord: Do not let the false prophets among you persuade you, and do not let your diviners persuade you. Do not listen to your dreams that you dream,
source_unit.display_text: Because thus said the Lord: Do not let the false prophets among you persuade you, and do not let your diviners persuade you. Do not listen to your dreams that you dream,

target_units.text: And do not listen to your false prophets, those divining for you, those dreaming for you, your omens, or your enchantments, who say: You will certainly not work for Babylon’s king.
target_units.display_text: And do not listen to your false prophets, those divining for you, those dreaming for you, your omens, or your enchantments, who say: You will certainly not work for Babylon’s king.

complete_triples.relationship: speaking in God's name without being sent
complete_triples.rationale: The letter denies that the Lord sent those prophesying unjust things in His name. Jeremiah 23 likewise distinguishes the prophets' running and speaking from any sending or speech by the Lord. Claimed prophetic activity is not treated as proof of commission.

source_unit.text: because they prophesy unjust things to you in My name, and I did not send them.
source_unit.display_text: because they prophesy unjust things to you in My name, and I did not send them.

target_units.text: I was not sending the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.
target_units.display_text: I was not sending the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.

complete_triples.relationship: seventy years and the announced return
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah connects Babylon's seventy years with divine visitation and return. Chronicles explicitly links the exile's seventy years and Cyrus's proclamation with fulfillment of the Lord's word through Jeremiah. This is an explicit narrative reception of the promised period and restoration.

source_unit.text: Because thus said the Lord: When seventy years are about to be fulfilled for Babylon, I will visit you and establish My words for you, to return your people to this place.
source_unit.display_text: Because thus said the Lord: When seventy years are about to be fulfilled for Babylon, I will visit you and establish My words for you, to return your people to this place.

target_units.text: He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,
target_units.display_text: He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,

target_units.text: to fulfill the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth, until the land accepted its Sabbaths, to keep Sabbath. All the days of its desolation it kept Sabbath, to complete seventy years.
target_units.display_text: to fulfill the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth, until the land accepted its Sabbaths, to keep Sabbath. All the days of its desolation it kept Sabbath, to complete seventy years.

target_units.display_text: “Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and He has commanded me to build Him a house in Jerusalem in Judea. Who among you is of all His people? His God shall be with him, and let him go up.”

complete_triples.relationship: explicit consultation of Jeremiah's seventy years
complete_triples.rationale: Daniel names Jeremiah while considering the books and a seventy-year term for Jerusalem's reproach. Jeremiah's letter also names a seventy-year period associated with Babylon and return. The explicit attribution links Daniel's reading with Jeremiah's temporal promise, without claiming he consulted this letter alone.

source_unit.text: Because thus said the Lord: When seventy years are about to be fulfilled for Babylon, I will visit you and establish My words for you, to return your people to this place.
source_unit.display_text: Because thus said the Lord: When seventy years are about to be fulfilled for Babylon, I will visit you and establish My words for you, to return your people to this place.

target_units.text: in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, considered in the books the number of years, when a command came to the land concerning Jeremiah the prophet, to bring Jerusalem’s reproach to its full term: seventy years.
target_units.display_text: in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, considered in the books the number of years, when a command came to the land concerning Jeremiah the prophet, to bring Jerusalem’s reproach to its full term: seventy years.

complete_triples.relationship: good intentions for the deportees
complete_triples.rationale: The letter announces a plan of peace rather than evils. The good-fig interpretation likewise promises the deportees good, restoration to their land and a heart to know the Lord. Both address the exiled community with a favorable divine intention beyond its displacement.

source_unit.text: And I will plan for you a plan of peace and not evils, to give you these things.
source_unit.display_text: And I will plan for you a plan of peace and not evils, to give you these things.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Like these good figs, so I will acknowledge Judah’s deportees, whom I have sent from this place to the Chaldeans’ land, for good things.
target_units.display_text: Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Like these good figs, so I will acknowledge Judah’s deportees, whom I have sent from this place to the Chaldeans’ land, for good things.

target_units.text: And I will fix My eyes upon them for good things and restore them to this land for good things. I will rebuild them and certainly not tear them down, plant them and certainly not pluck them out.
target_units.display_text: And I will fix My eyes upon them for good things and restore them to this land for good things. I will rebuild them and certainly not tear them down, plant them and certainly not pluck them out.

target_units.text: And I will give them a heart to know Me, that I am the Lord. They will be My people and I will be their God, because they will return to Me from their whole heart.
target_units.display_text: And I will give them a heart to know Me, that I am the Lord. They will be My people and I will be their God, because they will return to Me from their whole heart.

complete_triples.relationship: prayer answered by divine listening
complete_triples.rationale: The Lord invites prayer and promises to listen. Isaiah similarly promises listening before the people cry out and a response while they speak. The connection is the stated responsiveness to prayer; Isaiah intensifies its immediacy.

source_unit.text: And pray to Me, and I will listen to you.
source_unit.display_text: And pray to Me, and I will listen to you.

target_units.text: Before they cry out I will listen to them; while they are still speaking I will say, ‘What is it?’
target_units.display_text: Before they cry out I will listen to them; while they are still speaking I will say, ‘What is it?’

complete_triples.relationship: wholehearted seeking after displacement
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises finding the Lord when sought with the whole heart. Deuteronomy likewise promises finding Him through wholehearted seeking in distress, followed by return and covenant mercy. The shared wording fits the exile setting of Jeremiah's letter.

source_unit.text: And seek Me earnestly, and you will find Me, because you will seek Me with your whole heart,
source_unit.display_text: And seek Me earnestly, and you will find Me, because you will seek Me with your whole heart,

target_units.text: And there you shall seek the Lord your God, and shall find Him, when you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul, in your distress.
And all these things shall find you in the latter days, and you shall return unto the Lord your God, and hearken unto His voice.
For the Lord your God is a merciful God; He will not forsake you, neither will He destroy you, nor forget the covenant of your fathers which He sware unto them.

complete_triples.relationship: judgment upon speakers of uncommanded oracles
complete_triples.rationale: Ahab and Zedekiah are handed to Babylon's king to be struck, and the following units explain their unauthorized oracles. Deuteronomy announces death for a prophet speaking in God's name without His command. The connection concerns this stated offense and judgment, not other kings bearing the same names.

source_unit.text: Thus said the Lord concerning Ahab and Zedekiah: Behold, I am giving them into Babylon’s king’s hands, and he will strike them before your eyes.
source_unit.display_text: Thus said the Lord concerning Ahab and Zedekiah: Behold, I am giving them into Babylon’s king’s hands, and he will strike them before your eyes.

target_units.text: But the prophet who shall act ungodly, speaking in My name a word which I commanded him not to speak, or who shall speak in the name of other gods, that prophet shall die.

complete_triples.relationship: judged people becoming a curse expression
complete_triples.rationale: Judah's deportees will use the fate of Ahab and Zedekiah in a curse formula. Jeremiah's bad-fig oracle likewise announces people becoming a curse and reproach where they are scattered. The named pair provides a specific narrated form of that public disgrace.

source_unit.text: And all Judah’s deportees in Babylon will take a curse from them, saying: May the Lord make you as He made Zedekiah and Ahab, whom Babylon’s king fried in fire,
source_unit.display_text: And all Judah’s deportees in Babylon will take a curse from them, saying: May the Lord make you as He made Zedekiah and Ahab, whom Babylon’s king fried in fire,

target_units.text: And I will give them to scattering into all the earth’s kingdoms, and they will become a reproach, a parable, an object of hatred, and a curse in every place where I drove them out.
target_units.display_text: And I will give them to scattering into all the earth’s kingdoms, and they will become a reproach, a parable, an object of hatred, and a curse in every place where I drove them out.

complete_triples.relationship: adultery and lying within prophetic wrongdoing
complete_triples.rationale: The charge against Ahab and Zedekiah combines adultery with unauthorized speech in the Lord's name. Jeremiah 23 also joins adultery and walking in lies among Jerusalem's prophets. The shared offenses are explicit, while the locations and named offenders differ.

source_unit.text: because of the lawlessness they committed in Israel: they committed adultery with their fellow citizens’ wives and delivered an oracle in My name that I did not command them. I am a witness, says the Lord.
source_unit.display_text: because of the lawlessness they committed in Israel: they committed adultery with their fellow citizens’ wives and delivered an oracle in My name that I did not command them. I am a witness, says the Lord.

target_units.text: And among Jerusalem’s prophets I have seen horrifying things: committing adultery, walking in lies, and supporting evil hands so that no one turns from his evil way. They all became like Sodom to Me, and her inhabitants like Gomorrah.
target_units.display_text: And among Jerusalem’s prophets I have seen horrifying things: committing adultery, walking in lies, and supporting evil hands so that no one turns from his evil way. They all became like Sodom to Me, and her inhabitants like Gomorrah.

complete_triples.relationship: Zephaniah son of Maaseiah identified as priest
complete_triples.rationale: This address names Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest. Jeremiah 21 names the same priest as one of Zedekiah's messengers to Jeremiah. The matching personal name, father and office provide the connection without rewriting the unusual wording of the letter passage.

source_unit.text: I did not send you in My name. And to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest say:
source_unit.display_text: I did not send you in My name. And to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest say:

target_units.text: The word that came from the Lord to Jeremiah when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, saying:
target_units.display_text: The word that came from the Lord to Jeremiah when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, saying:

complete_triples.relationship: priestly confinement of a prophetic speaker
complete_triples.rationale: The letter describes priestly oversight placing a person prophesying into confinement and a trap. Jeremiah 20 narrates Pashhur, a temple leader, striking Jeremiah and putting him into a trap. The narrative supplies a concrete parallel to the described coercive practice, without identifying the two priests.

source_unit.text: The Lord appointed you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, to become an overseer in the Lord’s house over every person prophesying and every person raging, and you will put him into confinement and into the trap.
source_unit.display_text: The Lord appointed you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, to become an overseer in the Lord’s house over every person prophesying and every person raging, and you will put him into confinement and into the trap.

target_units.text: And Pashhur son of Immer, the priest who had been appointed leader of the Lord’s house, heard Jeremiah prophesying these words.
target_units.display_text: And Pashhur son of Immer, the priest who had been appointed leader of the Lord’s house, heard Jeremiah prophesying these words.

target_units.text: And he struck him and put him into the trap, which was at the gate of the separated upper house that was in the Lord’s house.
target_units.display_text: And he struck him and put him into the trap, which was at the gate of the separated upper house that was in the Lord’s house.

complete_triples.relationship: Jeremiah's association with Anathoth
complete_triples.rationale: The question names Jeremiah from Anathoth as the prophet being reviled. The book's opening identifies Jeremiah son of Hilkiah among priests living in Anathoth in Benjamin. That personal and local identification supports the link; the question is preserved as joining in reviling him.

source_unit.text: And now why did you join in reviling Jeremiah from Anathoth, who prophesied to you?
source_unit.display_text: And now why did you join in reviling Jeremiah from Anathoth, who prophesied to you?

target_units.display_text: The word of God that came upon Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests, who lived in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin,

complete_triples.relationship: same-chapter repetition of the letter's settlement instruction
complete_triples.rationale: The later question quotes Jeremiah's instruction to build houses, dwell in them, plant gardens and eat their fruit. Those are the instructions given earlier in the letter. This is a same-chapter literary repetition showing the specific advice recalled by the later question.

source_unit.text: Was it not for this that he sent to you in Babylon, saying: It is far off. Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens, and you will eat their fruit?
source_unit.display_text: Was it not for this that he sent to you in Babylon, saying: It is far off. Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens, and you will eat their fruit?

target_units.text: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruits,
target_units.display_text: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruits,

complete_triples.relationship: Shemaiah and Hananiah charged with the same deception
complete_triples.rationale: The Lord denies sending Shemaiah and says he made hearers trust unjust things. Jeremiah's charge against Hananiah likewise denies his commission and names trust in injustice. The wording connects two distinct false prophets, without merging their messages or fates.

source_unit.text: Send to the deportees, saying: Thus said the Lord concerning Shemaiah the Nelamite: Since Shemaiah prophesied to you, though I did not send him, and made you trust in unjust things,
source_unit.display_text: Send to the deportees, saying: Thus said the Lord concerning Shemaiah the Nelamite: Since Shemaiah prophesied to you, though I did not send him, and made you trust in unjust things,

target_units.text: And Jeremiah said to Hananiah: The Lord has not sent you, and you made this people trust in injustice.
target_units.display_text: And Jeremiah said to Hananiah: The Lord has not sent you, and you made this people trust in injustice.

complete_triples.relationship: exclusion from seeing promised good
complete_triples.rationale: Shemaiah and his family will not see the good the Lord will do for the deportees. Deuteronomy likewise excludes the judged men from seeing the good land promised to their fathers. Both use exclusion from a promised good as judgment, with different groups and circumstances.

source_unit.text: therefore thus said the Lord: Behold, I will visit Shemaiah and his family, and none of them will be among you to see the good things I will do for you. They will not see.
source_unit.display_text: therefore thus said the Lord: Behold, I will visit Shemaiah and his family, and none of them will be among you to see the good things I will do for you. They will not see.

target_units.text: And the Lord heard the voice of your words, and, being provoked to anger, sware, saying:
Surely none of these men shall see this good land which I sware unto their fathers,

complete_triples.relationship: prophetic words preserved in writing
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah is commanded to write all the delivered oracles in a book. Isaiah likewise receives a command to write on a tablet and in a book for enduring times. Both make a lasting written record part of the prophetic task.

source_unit.text: Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God: Write in a book all the words I delivered to you as oracles,
source_unit.display_text: Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God: Write in a book all the words I delivered to you as oracles,

target_units.text: Now then, sit and write these things on a tablet and in a book, because these things will endure for days of appointed times and for ever.
target_units.display_text: Now then, sit and write these things on a tablet and in a book, because these things will endure for days of appointed times and for ever.

complete_triples.relationship: Israel and Judah gathered into their land
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises the return of Israel's and Judah's deportees to the ancestral land. Ezekiel describes gathering Israel from the nations into that land and ending its division into two kingdoms. Both place restoration in a gathered people inhabiting the land again.

source_unit.text: because behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will return the deportees of My people Israel and Judah, said the Lord. I will return them to the land I gave their fathers, and they will rule over it.
source_unit.display_text: because behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will return the deportees of My people Israel and Judah, said the Lord. I will return them to the land I gave their fathers, and they will rule over it.

target_units.text: and say to them, Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am taking all Israel’s house from among the nations where they entered, gathering them from all those around them and bringing them into Israel’s land.
target_units.display_text: and say to them, Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am taking all Israel’s house from among the nations where they entered, gathering them from all those around them and bringing them into Israel’s land.

target_units.text: I will make them one nation in My land and upon Israel’s mountains, and one ruler will be theirs. They will no longer be two nations or ever again be divided into two kingdoms,
target_units.display_text: I will make them one nation in My land and upon Israel’s mountains, and one ruler will be theirs. They will no longer be two nations or ever again be divided into two kingdoms,

complete_triples.relationship: peace absent amid approaching calamity
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah announces a sound of fear and no peace. The earlier lament reports gathering for peace but finding no good, and looking for healing but finding haste. Both describe the absence of expected security; the target's final word is preserved as haste, not changed to terror.

source_unit.text: Thus said the Lord: You will hear a sound of fear—fear, and there is no peace.
source_unit.display_text: Thus said the Lord: You will hear a sound of fear—fear, and there is no peace.

target_units.text: We gathered for peace, and there were no good things; for a time of healing, and behold, haste!
target_units.display_text: We gathered for peace, and there were no good things; for a time of healing, and behold, haste!

complete_triples.relationship: fear pictured through childbirth pains and altered faces
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah portrays people holding their loins and faces turning toward jaundice, while asking whether a male gives birth. Isaiah describes labor pains like a woman giving birth and faces changing toward flame. The shared physical imagery expresses fear, while the facial descriptions differ.

source_unit.text: Ask and see whether a male gave birth, and about fear in which they will hold loins and salvation. For I have seen every person with his hands upon his loins; faces turned toward jaundice—
source_unit.display_text: Ask and see whether a male gave birth, and about fear in which they will hold loins and salvation. For I have seen every person with his hands upon his loins; faces turned toward jaundice—

target_units.display_text: Therefore every hand will slacken, and every human soul grow cowardly;

target_units.text: the envoys will be troubled, and labor pains will hold them like those of a woman giving birth. They will lament to one another and be distraught, and change their face as to flame.
target_units.display_text: the envoys will be troubled, and labor pains will hold them like those of a woman giving birth. They will lament to one another and be distraught, and change their face as to flame.

complete_triples.relationship: unprecedented affliction with a favorable announced outcome
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah calls Jacob's narrow time a great day without equal and promises he will be saved from it. Daniel also describes an unparalleled day of affliction and an outcome for the people inscribed in the book. Daniel's supplied verb is exalted; the passages are not identified as the same dated event.

source_unit.text: so it became. For that day is great, and there is none like it; it is a narrow time for Jacob, and he will be saved from it.
source_unit.display_text: so it became. For that day is great, and there is none like it; it is a narrow time for Jacob, and he will be saved from it.

target_units.text: “At that hour Michael will pass by, the great angel who stands over the sons of your people. That will be a day of affliction such as has not occurred since they came into being until that day. On that day all the people found inscribed in the book will be exalted.
target_units.display_text: “At that hour Michael will pass by, the great angel who stands over the sons of your people. That will be a day of affliction such as has not occurred since they came into being until that day. On that day all the people found inscribed in the book will be exalted.

complete_triples.relationship: the removal of an oppressive yoke
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises that the yoke and bonds will be broken and foreign service cease. Isaiah likewise announces removal and destruction of the yoke from the people's shoulders. Both portray relief from oppression through a removed yoke, with distinct immediate enemy settings.

source_unit.text: On that day, said the Lord, I will smash the yoke from their neck and tear apart their bonds, and they will no longer work for foreigners.
source_unit.display_text: On that day, said the Lord, I will smash the yoke from their neck and tear apart their bonds, and they will no longer work for foreigners.

target_units.text: On that day his fear will be removed from you and his yoke from your shoulder, and the yoke will be destroyed from your shoulders.
target_units.display_text: On that day his fear will be removed from you and his yoke from your shoulder, and the yoke will be destroyed from your shoulders.

complete_triples.relationship: David raised as ruler with the Lord as God
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah joins service to the Lord with David their king being raised for them. Ezekiel likewise promises to raise David as shepherd and calls him ruler while the Lord is their God. The corresponding combination of divine allegiance and Davidic rule is explicit.

source_unit.text: And they will work for the Lord their God, and I will raise up David their king for them.
source_unit.display_text: And they will work for the Lord their God, and I will raise up David their king for them.

target_units.text: I will raise up one shepherd over them, My servant David, and he will shepherd them and be their shepherd.
target_units.display_text: I will raise up one shepherd over them, My servant David, and he will shepherd them and be their shepherd.

target_units.text: I, the Lord, will be their God, and David a ruler among them. I, the Lord, have spoken.
target_units.display_text: I, the Lord, will be their God, and David a ruler among them. I, the Lord, have spoken.

complete_triples.relationship: return to the Lord and David their king
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah announces service to the Lord and a raised Davidic king. Hosea similarly says Israel's sons will return and seek the Lord their God and David their king. Both associate Israel's renewed allegiance with David, without specifying how the royal promise is to be realized.

source_unit.text: And they will work for the Lord their God, and I will raise up David their king for them.
source_unit.display_text: And they will work for the Lord their God, and I will raise up David their king for them.

complete_triples.relationship: communal injury without effective healing
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah says treatment has brought pain and no benefit. The earlier lament asks whether Gilead lacks resin or a physician because healing has not arisen for the people. Both present the community's injury as remaining without effective remedy.

complete_triples.relationship: abandonment by former friends amid suffering
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah says all the friends have forgotten and will not inquire after the stricken people. Lamentations describes Jerusalem without comfort among those who love her, with friends becoming enemies. Both add failed human support to the people's affliction.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah's reversal includes enemies eating their flesh and plunderers becoming plunder. complete_triples.rationale: The Lord promises a cure and healing for the painful wound of the one called Scattered. Jeremiah 40 likewise promises the closing of wounds, remedy and healing for the city. The later oracle repeats this image of restoration through healing.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah links returned deportees with a city rebuilt on its height and the sanctuary's restoration. Ezekiel promises inhabited cities, rebuilt devastation and settlement as at the beginning. Both connect the people's return with the recovery of their built environment.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises singers and people playing as the community increases. The psalm describes captivity reversed and mouths filled with joy and exultation. complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises the sons' return as formerly and visitation upon those afflicting them. Isaiah joins the Lord's judgment of the people's case with rescuing their sons. Both place the children's welfare alongside divine action against their adversity.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah says the ruler will come from the people being restored. Deuteronomy requires a ruler from among the people's brothers and excludes a foreigner. complete_triples.relationship: recurring imagery of swirling divine anger
complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah again describes the Lord's anger going out in a swirling movement upon the ungodly. Jeremiah 23 similarly describes anger emerging in a convulsion and swirling upon them. The distinctive movement and recipients connect the two formulations.

complete_triples.relationship: anger continuing until the divine undertaking is accomplished

complete_triples.relationship: the reciprocal God-and-people promise
complete_triples.rationale: The Lord promises to be God to Israel's family and that they will be His people. The good-fig oracle gives the same reciprocal promise to the returning deportees, together with a heart to know Him. Both describe restoration as a renewed relationship.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah joins eternal love with being drawn into compassion. Isaiah promises everlasting mercy after a short period of anger. Both emphasize enduring divine favor in restoration; Isaiah explicitly frames it against a preceding withdrawal.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah calls for renewed vineyard planting on Samaria's mountains. Amos describes Israel's reversed captivity, planted vineyards and enjoyment of their wine. complete_triples.rationale: The people set pollutions within the house over which the Lord's name is invoked. Jeremiah 7 likewise says Judah placed abominations in that named house to defile it. The shared place and act make this a close recurrence of the temple indictment.

complete_triples.rationale: The description of the city's threatened transfer names sword, famine and a sent affliction. complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises gathering from all the lands of angry dispersion and return to this place. Ezekiel likewise promises taking Israel from the surrounding nations and bringing them into Israel's land. Both describe a geographically gathered community after dispersion.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises that they will be His people and He their God. Ezekiel repeats the same reciprocal formula alongside the Lord's dwelling among them. The shared words define the relationship of the restored community in both oracles.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises another way and another heart so the people fear the Lord continually. Ezekiel likewise promises another heart and new spirit so they walk in His commands. complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises an eternal covenant and a heart that will not depart from the Lord. Ezekiel likewise promises an everlasting covenant of peace with holy things among the people for ever. Both express enduring commitment, while describing its effects differently.

complete_triples.rationale: The Lord promises attentive good and faithful planting in the land. The good-fig oracle likewise fixes His eyes upon the deportees for good and promises return, building and planting. The shared combination of favorable attention and secure reestablishment is explicit.

complete_triples.rationale: Jeremiah promises to bring the announced good just as He brought the great calamities. Jeremiah 38 similarly contrasts watching to tear down and harm with watching to build and plant. Both describe restoration through a deliberate reversal of previous divine action.

complete_triples.rationale: The promise that fields will again be acquired in the desolate, surrendered land reiterates the earlier assurance that fields, houses and vineyards will be acquired again. amended_full_triples_reread.relationship: narrative parallel of seizure amid temple accusations
amended_full_triples_reread.rationale: Jeremiah is seized after delivering the temple oracle and threatened with death. Stephen is also seized, with witnesses accusing him of speaking against the holy place and its destruction. The accounts share seizure amid temple controversy; Acts explicitly calls Stephen's witnesses false.

The oracle states that the remaining vessels will go to Babylon. Kings narrates the Chaldeans removing temple bronze and other utensils, explicitly carrying the bronze to Babylon. The narrative provides a corresponding removal of temple property in contrast to the false assurances of its return.

Jeremiah 37 also promises a broken yoke and ended foreign service, within a restoration oracle. The shared liberation image does not authenticate Hananiah's timetable or his claim to have been sent.

Those are the instructions given earlier in the letter. This is a same-chapter literary repetition showing the specific advice recalled by the later question.

amended_full_triples_reread.relationship: unprecedented affliction with a favorable announced outcome
amended_full_triples_reread.rationale: Jeremiah calls Jacob's narrow time a great day without equal and promises he will be saved from it. Daniel also describes an unparalleled day of affliction and an outcome for the people inscribed in the book. Daniel's supplied verb is exalted; the passages are not identified as the same dated event.

amended_full_triples_reread.relationship: abandonment by former friends amid suffering
amended_full_triples_reread.rationale: Jeremiah says all the friends have forgotten and will not inquire after the stricken people. Lamentations describes Jerusalem without comfort among those who love her, with friends becoming enemies. Both add failed human support to the people's affliction.

Jeremiah's reversal includes enemies eating their flesh and plunderers becoming plunder. Isaiah likewise says the afflicters will eat their own flesh and says all flesh will recognize the Lord as rescuer. The unusual flesh-consuming image gives this connection a specific basis beyond a general reversal of fortunes.

amended_full_triples_reread.rationale: The Lord promises a cure and healing for the painful wound of the one called Scattered. Jeremiah 40 likewise promises the closing of wounds, remedy and healing for the city. The later oracle repeats this image of restoration through healing.

Both make restored cultivation a concrete feature of the people's return, while identifying different geographical details.

Jeremiah foresees returned captivity and an acclamation blessing the Lord over His righteous, holy mountain. Zechariah likewise describes the Lord returning to Zion and the mountain being called holy. Both link renewed presence in Jerusalem's setting with the mountain's holiness.

Jeremiah describes the Lord filling thirsty and hungry souls. The psalm similarly says the Lord filled an empty soul and a hungry soul with good things. The explicit filling of the hungry provides the link; the psalm's first description is empty rather than thirsty.

amended_full_triples_reread.rationale: Hebrews repeats the absence of neighbor-to-neighbor teaching to know the Lord, knowledge from least to greatest and forgiveness with sins no longer remembered. The full sequence follows Jeremiah's promise, making this an explicit citation rather than a generic forgiveness theme.

amended_full_triples_reread.rationale: Jeremiah's prayer says the people received the land but failed to hear and obey, and that God caused the calamities to befall them.
